opus-5.5.text:
Well, I come from physics, and in physics the way you know you understand something is that you can make a quantitative prediction that could have turned out to be wrong. In deep learning there are a lot of qualitative stories. People say the network learns hierarchical features, or it exploits invariances, or it avoids the curse of dimensionality. These stories may well be right, but in that form they're very hard to falsify. You can almost always tell a story after the fact.

So what I like to do is build simplified models of data, toy models if you want, that still capture something essential about real data. For example, generative models with a hierarchical, compositional structure, a bit like a grammar. These models have parameters: the number of features at each level, how many ways a higher-level feature can be made from lower-level ones, the depth, and so on. Then you can ask very concrete questions. How many training examples do you need before the network starts to represent a latent variable at a certain level of the hierarchy? How does the test error decay with the size of the training set? And you get a scaling law, an exponent, that depends on those parameters.

That's powerful for two reasons. First, it's a sharp test. If your theory says the sample complexity scales as some power of the number of features, you change that number in experiments and either the curves collapse the way you predicted or they don't. It's not something you can wiggle out of. Second, it links to what people actually observe at scale. Empirical scaling laws in language and vision are one of the few robust quantitative facts we have about deep learning. If your toy model produces power laws, and you can explain where the exponents come from in terms of the structure of the data, you start to have a mechanistic explanation rather than just a curve fit.

There's also a more conceptual point. The parameters let you find the crossover, the regime where something qualitatively changes, like when a network goes from behaving like a kernel method to really learning features, or when it suddenly becomes able to exploit the hierarchical structure. That's very much a statistical physics way of thinking: you look for the relevant variables and the phase diagram. Once you have that, you understand not just that the method works, but when it works, why, and what would break it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes testing predicted scaling by varying model parameters and checking whether experimental curves collapse as predicted, but it does not identify plotting results on log–log axes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes from my background in physics, really. In physics we have this tradition where you don't just make a qualitative story, you build a model, a toy model usually, with a few parameters, and the model makes predictions. And the most valuable predictions are scaling predictions: how does some quantity, say the test error, behave as a function of the number of data points, or the dimension, or the width of the network. Because a scaling law, an exponent, is something very constraining. If I tell you that the error decays like the number of samples to the minus one-half, or to the minus one over the dimension, these are completely different claims, and you can go and check them. You cannot fool yourself for very long.

And this matters a lot in deep learning, because the field is full of plausible stories. You can always tell a nice story about why something works, and the story may be completely wrong, and you would never know. Whereas if your theory predicts an exponent, and you measure an exponent, and they don't match, then the theory is dead, or at least it needs to be fixed. That's healthy. It's the way to make progress.

The other thing is that these simplified models, with a few parameters, let you understand what the relevant variables actually are. Real networks have millions of hyperparameters, in a sense, and you can't explore all of that. But if you have a model where you can say, okay, the key control parameter is the ratio of the number of parameters to the number of data points, or it's how far the weights move from initialization, then you can build an understanding, a kind of phase diagram, and then test whether the real systems fall in the same picture. So for me the model is not meant to be realistic. It's meant to capture one mechanism, and the scaling prediction is the way you check that the mechanism is really there.

astra-6.text:
Because they force you to make a quantitative prediction. If I propose a mechanism, I want to know more than whether it produces a curve that looks roughly like the data. I want to know: if I change the number of samples, or the size of the model, how should the outcome change?

Scaling predictions are useful because they can distinguish explanations that look very similar in one setting. You might fit a particular observation with several models, but those models can predict different behavior as you vary a parameter. Then you have a way to test which ingredients matter.

The model doesn't have to capture everything. Ideally, it's simple enough that you can understand why the prediction follows. And if the prediction fails, that's useful too: it tells you something is missing from your explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
Because then you can be wrong in a precise way. If you have a qualitative explanation, it’s often quite easy to accommodate whatever you observe afterward. But if your model predicts how something scales with the number of samples, or the number of parameters, then you have a much stronger test. You can vary those quantities and see whether the prediction holds.

For me, the point of a simple model is not to reproduce every detail. It’s to isolate a mechanism and derive consequences that you wouldn’t have put in by hand. And if the scaling is wrong, that’s useful: it tells you that some assumption is missing or that the mechanism is not the relevant one.
